adversarial_test_results.detail: ' am' appears as the ordinary first-person copula rather than the first piece of a rare drug name, which the hypothesis places at baseline (its separately noted expletive-subject copula family does not cover 'I am').

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Ham radio operators gathered on the hill for the annual field day.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' Ham' is kept token-identical but appears in the common-noun compound 'Ham radio', not as the first piece of a proper name, so the hypothesis predicts no response.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The soldiers will march past the monument at dawn tomorrow.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' march' is the lowercase verb rather than the capitalized month name the hypothesis singles out, so the same surface word in another sense should stay at baseline.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Our deepest sympathy goes out to everyone affected by the flooding.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: We compared the two proposals carefully before choosing the cheaper vendor.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'compared' stands in its plain verbal sense and introduces no specific value, so the hypothesis predicts baseline despite it being a claimed activating token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The governing body approved the annual budget at its quarterly meeting.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Rain had fallen through the night, and by morning the yard behind the workshop had turned to mud. The crew arrived early anyway, carrying their bags across the wet ground and setting up under the narrow shelter that ran along the side of the building. Nobody said much at first. There was coffee in a thermos, and someone had brought a box of pastries that were already going stale.

The work itself was slow and repetitive. Each board had to be measured, marked, and cut, and each cut had to be checked against the plan before the next one began. The older workers moved with an economy that the younger ones envied, never reaching for a tool they did not need. By noon the stack of finished pieces had grown about as tall as the bench, and the noise of the saws had settled into a rhythm that nobody noticed anymore.

Lunch was eaten outside, standing up, because the shelter was too crowded to sit in. The talk turned to the weather, then to a dispute about a shared fence that had been going on for two seasons, and then to nothing in particular. The afternoon passed in the same unhurried way. Somebody put on a radio, then turned it off again when the signal drifted into static. When the light began to fail, the crew swept the shavings into a pile, covered the machines, and walked out to the road one by one.

The foreman stayed behind. He walked the length of the finished section, running a hand along the joints, checking the line with his eye the way he had been taught as a boy. Everything was where it should be. He locked the door, turned off the lights, and stood for a moment in the quiet, listening to water dripping from the eaves.

The next morning the inspector arrived with a case of instruments and a clipboard of forms. She worked methodically, testing each joint and noting every reading in a small, cramped hand. It was the sort of inspection that could end a season's work or quietly pass it, and the crew stood at a distance, pretending not to watch. When she had finished the last section she knelt beside the stone foundation, opened a vial, and swept a swab across the mortar. Later, the lab would confirm the presence of benzalkonium chloride in the sample, a detail that would matter more than any of the readings she had taken before.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context holdout: roughly 450 words of plain narrative prose with no numerals, proper names or claimed trigger tokens, ending in a rare technical term ('benzalkonium chloride') introduced into a slot, testing whether the response survives depth and length.
